newsitem.title: UK: NatWest completes housing association loans sale.
newsitem.headline: NatWest completes housing association loans sale.

text.p: The sell-off of British housing association loans was completed on Monday with the launch of a one billion stg ($1.6 billion) securitisation.
NatWest Markets, the investment banking arm of National Westminster Bank Plc, arranged a seven-tranche bond issue for a special funding vehicle called Finance for Residential Housing plc (FRESH).
The bonds will be secured by a portfolio of 38,000 loans made to around 1,000 housing associations.
The loans were previously owned by The Housing Corporation and Housing for Wales, bodies regulating housing associations.
NatWest bought these loans after an open bidding contest.
British institions were the main investors in the deal.
"Demand is coming from UK institutions. The average life (28.6 years) fits very well with their need to invest long-term liabilities from pension and life insurance," a banker at NatWest said.

The issue size of the bond was 972 million pounds, with the largest tranche amounting to 727 million pounds. These notes carry a top triple-A rating from four rating agencies, but still offered a 60 basis point spread over long-dated gilt yields.
The FRESH deal does not carry a government guarantee but NatWest said the highly-rated bonds provided an alternative to British government paper.
"This is seen as a good substitute for gilts. Social housing will not go away and one would assume will always require some sort of government support," the NatWest banker said.
"Housing associations have a long history of providing social housing and collecting rent and that rent is in turn subsidised by housing benefit paid by the government," he said.
The British election due on May 1 and expected to result in a change of government to Labour from Conservative would not affect the deal, he said. The payment date is March 26.
Housing association loans mark the latest sizeable deal in the government's drive to transfer as much funding as possible from public to private hands.
A similar transaction last October saw a consortium which owned British Ministry of Defence living quarters issue a 900 million pound bond backed by rental incomes.
